Brotherly Love
BRUHþH-er-lee LUV
n.
Brotherly + love; renders the Greek philadelphia, “love of the brethren,” from philos (loving) + adelphos (brother).

Biblical Definition

Brotherly love is the warm, settled, practical love of the saints for one another as brothers—the love proper to the new family God has constituted in Christ, where the bond is not biological but blood-bought and the affection is not optional but commanded. The Greek philadelphia is a near-technical New Testament term: let brotherly love continue (Heb 13:1); be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10); but as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another (1 Thess 4:9); add to your faith virtue... and to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity (2 Pet 1:5-7); seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently (1 Pet 1:22). Brotherly love is therefore the affectionate, practical, sustained love among Christians that springs from the recognition of shared sonship to the same Father, shared Lordship of the same Christ, shared indwelling of the same Spirit, and shared inheritance in the same kingdom. It expresses itself in hospitality (Heb 13:1-2), in burden-bearing (Gal 6:2), in mutual exhortation (Heb 3:13), in supplying one another’s needs (Acts 4:34; 1 John 3:17), in honor-preferring (Rom 12:10), in forbearance and forgiveness (Eph 4:32; Col 3:13), and in the laying down of life for the brethren in extreme cases (1 John 3:16). It is to be both fervent (1 Pet 1:22, ektenōs, stretched-out) and unfeigned (1 Pet 1:22, anupokritos, without hypocrisy)—hot in its actual warmth and pure in its genuineness, no performance and no mask. The visible and verifiable presence of brotherly love among Christians is named by Christ Himself as the credential of His disciples to the watching world: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BROTHERLY LOVE as the affection which is proper to brothers; in religion, the love which Christians ought to entertain for each other as members of the family of Christ.

expand to see more

BROTHERLY, a. — 1. Pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers. 2. Becoming brothers; affectionate; kind; as, brotherly love.

LOVE, n. — In a general sense, that strong affection of the mind which arises from the perception of agreeable qualities in any object, or which is excited by some good received. In a religious sense, the love which Christians bear to God and to one another as members of the family of Christ (1 John 4:7-21).

Key Scripture

Hebrews 13:1 — "Let brotherly love continue."

Romans 12:10 — "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another."

1 Peter 1:22 — "Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently."

John 13:35 — "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another."

Modern Corruption

Brotherly love is corrupted by the affinity-grouped, online-mediated, low-cost-friendly version of contemporary church life that has substituted shared interests, theological agreement, or social comfort for the cross-cultural, costly, commanded love of the brethren the New Testament describes.

expand to see more

The contemporary church has often substituted affinity-grouped affiliation for the New Testament’s brotherly love. Believers gather along the lines of shared age, life-stage, social class, education, political tribe, and theological niche—and within these comfortable affinities they exhibit a real but limited warmth. The New Testament’s vision is sharper. The brotherly love commanded crosses every natural human grouping precisely because the brotherhood is constituted by Christ and not by natural affinity: rich and poor, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, the educated and the unlettered, the temperamentally compatible and the temperamentally jarring are all brothers in the same family, and the brotherly love commanded extends across all the lines natural affinity would draw. Recover the doctrine, and the church recovers a love that demonstrates the gospel: the visible, cross-natural love of saints who would not otherwise be together but who love each other in Christ.

The companion corruption is the online-mediated and low-cost-friendly version that has reduced brotherly love to the digital affirmations of a Sunday community and the polite social presence of weekly attendance. The New Testament’s brotherly love is costly: it bears the burdens that take time, energy, and money to bear (Gal 6:2); it supplies the actual needs that close brothers and sisters in real distress (1 John 3:17); it lays down its life when love calls for that extremity (1 John 3:16); it forgives the actual offenses that close-up life-together inevitably produces (Eph 4:32); it forbears with the real frictions of imperfect saints in real proximity (Eph 4:2). The recovery is the recovery of embodied, costly, sustained brotherly love among the saints of one’s actual local church: bear the burdens you actually see, supply the needs you actually know of, forgive the brother who has actually offended, lay down what needs to be laid down. The credential Christ named—by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples—is given to a church living that pattern, not to one performing a digital affiliation.

Hebrew Roots

Greek philadelphia (love of the brethren, from philos + adelphos): the affectionate, sustained, practical love of the saints for one another as the new family God has constituted in Christ.

expand to see more

Greek philadelphia (G5360) — love of the brethren (Rom 12:10; 1 Thess 4:9; Heb 13:1; 1 Pet 1:22; 2 Pet 1:7).

Greek adelphos (G80) — brother (the family-of-faith vocabulary of the NT).

Greek ektenōs (G1619) — fervently, stretched-out (1 Pet 1:22).

Greek anupokritos (G505) — unfeigned, without hypocrisy (1 Pet 1:22; Rom 12:9; 1 Tim 1:5).

Usage

"Let brotherly love continue—Hebrews 13:1 commands the discipline as the saint’s standing posture in the body."

"Brotherly love is the credential of Christ’s disciples: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another."

"Affinity-grouped affiliation and online-mediated friendliness substitute for the cross-natural, embodied, costly brotherly love the New Testament describes."
